Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: 'Being looked at sexually' is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision as the index trauma, especially when no other selected items suggest sexual trauma, harassment, or body-focused threat. This trigger appears trauma-incongruent.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Listening for signs that someone is entering the home implies an interpersonal intrusion/assault threat, which does not fit well with a motor vehicle collision and is not supported by the other items. The rest of the threat profile is general hypervigilance to sudden sounds, making this specific home-intruder monitoring item clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes
issues.explanation: Avoiding similar clothes usually implies clothing cues tied to the trauma context. For a motor vehicle collision, this is difficult to justify unless other items indicate clothing-specific trauma reminders, which they do not. It also does not connect plausibly to the selected triggers, which are taste, workplace, and sexual objectification.

Workplace as a trigger is weakly grounded for a life-threatening motor vehicle collision given the rest of the profile: the other trigger and threat items are sensory/accident-related, but nothing in appraisals, threat, or strategies explains why the workplace itself would be a salient trauma cue. This makes the trigger set less coherent across nodes.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: A specific taste linked to a motor vehicle collision is possible but clinically unusual, and here it is unsupported by memory content or appraisals that would make a gustatory cue understandable. With no memory items and otherwise sound/crash/vehicle-focused content, this trigger stands out as poorly integrated with the formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, a specific taste trigger and an alcohol smell trigger are not impossible, but in combination they imply trauma details (e.g. ingestion, blood, alcohol involvement, hospital/chemical context) that are unsupported by the rest of the profile. The rest of the triggers, threat items, and appraisals are centered on vehicle crash/sound danger, so these sensory triggers look clinically disconnected from the trauma representation described elsewhere.

Undereating as a coping strategy is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The formulation strongly links triggers, threat, negative appraisals, and avoidance-based coping around crash-related distress; avoid-driving and screen escape fit that pattern, but food restriction addresses a symptom domain not otherwise represented in triggers, threat, memory, or appraisals. In this profile it appears clinically mismatched rather than a coherent extension of the same trauma-linked cycle.

vignette:
Omar remembers the exact shade of the other car: a deep, metallic blue, the kind that catches the evening light. It was that blue sedan that had barrelled through the red light eight months ago, the screech of tires drowned out by the sickening crunch of metal. In the disorienting moments that followed, as he sat pinned in his driver's seat, the most potent sensation was the smell. It wasn't just gasoline and burnt rubber; it was the cloying, sweet stench of whiskey rolling in through the shattered window from the other driver, who had stumbled out of his car, dazed and drunk. That specific combination-the image of his own crumpled hood, the sight of a dark blue sedan, the smell of alcohol-became the architecture of his fear.

In the weeks that followed, the world transformed into a landscape of potential threats. Omar, a man who had built a career as a tax inspector on meticulous observation and calm logic, now found himself in a constant state of high alert. Walking to the grocery store became an ordeal; he was superalert, his head swivelling at every intersection, his body tensed for an impact that never came. An unexpected sound, like a truck backfiring down the street or a neighbour dropping a heavy box, would make him jump violently, his heart hammering against his ribs as if the crash were happening all over again. He began to believe the world was fundamentally unsafe, and that his own senses were the only fragile defense he had left.

This pervasive sense of threat began to dismantle his life. Driving was the first thing to go. The thought of getting behind the wheel, or even sitting in a passenger seat, was unbearable. This created an immediate crisis at his job, which often required him to travel to businesses for audits. He was shifted to entirely desk-based work, a move that felt less like an accommodation and more like a demotion. He saw the shift as proof of a devastating new reality: he was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined him. The confident, competent professional felt like a ghost, a memory of someone he used to be. This belief calcified with every simple mistake he made on a tax form, his focus shattered by the slightest noise from the street outside his office window. He was certain he could no longer rely on himself.

At home, in the evenings, the silence was worse than the noise. It allowed the images of the accident to play on a loop. To fend them off, Omar would retreat into the small, bright screen of his phone, losing hours to mindless games and scrolling, anything to occupy the space in his head. His appetite withered along with his social life. He began restricting his food, the feeling of hunger a dull, manageable ache that distracted from the sharper pain of his anxiety. His ex-wife had called it "disappearing," and she wasn't wrong. He felt emotionally hollowed out, as if the crash had scooped out his capacity for joy, love, or even simple contentment, leaving only fear. He had come to believe he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, a conviction that made connection feel pointless.

It was a final performance review at work that finally brought him to seek help. His supervisor was gentle but firm: his desk-work productivity had plummeted, and his inability to perform site visits was unsustainable. Faced with the concrete possibility of losing the last pillar of his old identity, Omar felt a flicker of something beyond fear: desperation. He arrived at the clinic not with any real hope of recovery, but with the quiet, terrifying question of whether there was anything left of the man he once was, or if he had been permanently lost on that street corner eight months ago.
